Let's recall what the regression in Session 13 did before we start something new.

First. In Session 13 your regression predicted a number. Which number, and for what? Have a think.

It predicted weekly orders for a branch, using inputs such as footfall and rainfall. The answer was a number on a scale.

Second. Explaining and predicting are different jobs. Which one is today about? Sit with it for a second.

Predicting. Today we guess the outcome for a loan the computer has never seen. The answer is a yes or a no, and that change brings a new way of checking our work.

slides.title: A rule you write, and a rule found from examples

points: You show 8,000 past loans and what happened
The computer finds the rule itself
You test the rule on loans it has not seen

slides.verdict: In a spreadsheet you give the rule. In machine learning you give examples.
slides.notes:
Machine learning rests on one idea, and you already know half of it.

On the left is a spreadsheet rule. You write an IF formula. Flag the loan as risky when the instalment is more than sixty percent of income. The sixty percent came from your gut.

On the right, we hand the computer eight thousand past loans, with what happened to each one. It searches for a rule that fits those examples.

Then we check that rule on loans it has not seen. A rule that only works on the past is no use to a lender.

So the verdict is short. In a spreadsheet you give the rule. In machine learning you give examples, and you check the rule it finds.

slides.title: Meet the Nile Microfinance loans
slides.code:
import pandas as pd

loans = pd.read_csv('loans.csv')
print(loans.shape)
print(loans.default.mean())
print(loans.default.value_counts().to_dict())
says: Load the file, as in Session 7.
The mean of a column of 1s and 0s is the share of 1s.
Count the two answers: 0 repaid, 1 defaulted.
slides.notes:
Let's meet the data. Nile Microfinance is a fictional lender in Uganda, and this file has one row for each loan.

First we load it, exactly as we did with the orders in Session 7.

Eight thousand loans and eighteen columns. The last column is default. A one means the borrower defaulted, which means they stopped repaying. A zero means the loan was repaid.

A small trick helps here. The average of a column of ones and zeros is the share of ones. So the mean is point one two five five. About twelve and a half percent of these loans defaulted.

The counts say the same thing. Six thousand nine hundred and ninety six loans repaid, and one thousand and four defaulted.

slides.title: Only about one loan in eight defaults
look: Repaid loans tower over defaulted ones.
Defaulted loans are 1,004 of 8,000, about 12.5 percent.
One answer is far more common than the other.
slides.caption: Class imbalance: the answer we care about is the rare one.
slides.alt: Two bars showing most loans are repaid and about one in eight defaults.
slides.notes:
Here are those two counts as a picture. Remember this chart. It will matter again in a few minutes.

The tall bar is the repaid loans. Almost all of them.

The short bar is the defaulted loans, one thousand and four out of eight thousand. The chart rounds the share to twelve point six percent. The exact figure is twelve point five five, and we say about twelve and a half.

When one answer is far more common than the other, we say the data has class imbalance. Lenders live with this all the time. The loans that hurt are the ones that are rare.

Why does that matter? Give that a moment.

Because a lazy guesser who says repaid every time would be right almost nine times in ten. Hold that thought.

slides.title: Features go in, the target comes out
slides.lead: Every learning problem has two kinds of columns. Name them before you do anything else.

points.t: The input columns: age, income, loan amount, savings and so on.
The column to predict. Here it is default, 1 or 0.
One loan. The model learns from many rows with known targets.

slides.notes:
Two words to settle first, because the rest of today uses them.

A feature is an input column. Age, monthly income, loan amount, savings, how many earlier late payments. Anything we know about the borrower when the loan is made.

The target is the column we want to predict. Here that's default. Think of it as the cell you wish you could fill in before the loan is approved.

Each row is one loan. During learning, the computer sees the features and the known target for thousands of rows, and works out how the two are linked. Later it sees only the features of a new loan and has to guess the target.

slides.title: Fix the impossible ages first
slides.code:
print(loans.age.sort_values().head(3).tolist())
print(loans.age.sort_values().tail(3).tolist())

bad_age = (loans.age < 18) | (loans.age > 100)
print(bad_age.sum())
good_median = int(loans.loc[~bad_age, 'age'].median())
loans.loc[bad_age, 'age'] = good_median
print(loans.age.min(), loans.age.max())
says: Sorting shows a borrower aged 0 and one aged 199.
Mark any age under 18 or over 100 with a True and False test.
Replace those with the median of the good ages, which is 36.
slides.notes:
Models learn from whatever we give them, so we prepare the data first, with the pandas you already know.

Start with a look. Sort the ages and print the smallest and the largest three. The smallest is zero, and the largest is one hundred and ninety nine. Nobody is a hundred and ninety nine, and a lender does not lend to a newborn. Those are data entry errors.

We mark the bad ages with a True and False test, the boolean mask from Session 7. Under eighteen, or over a hundred. Two loans fail the test.

We replace them with the median of the good ages, which is thirty six. Ages now run from twenty to sixty eight. We changed only two rows out of eight thousand, and we know exactly which ones.

slides.title: Fill missing incomes and remember which ones
slides.code:
loans['income_missing'] = loans.monthly_income_ugx.isna().astype(int)
median_income = loans.monthly_income_ugx.median()
loans['monthly_income_ugx'] = loans.monthly_income_ugx.fillna(median_income)
print(median_income, loans.income_missing.sum())
says: Add a flag column: 1 where income was blank, 0 elsewhere.
Fill the blanks with the median income.
slides.notes:
Next, the missing incomes. Three hundred and seventy nine loans have a blank income.

A model cannot learn from a blank cell. Most scikit-learn models stop with an error that says the input contains NaN, which is the computer's word for missing. So we must fill them, and we must say how.

First we add a flag. That's a new column of ones and zeros that remembers which rows were blank. Filling hides the gap, and the flag keeps the memory of it. A missing income might itself tell us something.

Then we fill the blanks with the median income, six hundred and forty two thousand six hundred shillings. The median, because a few big earners would drag the mean up.

One detail you should know. We worked out the median using all eight thousand loans, before the split we make shortly. The effect is tiny. In Session 19 you'll learn a pipeline that does this the careful way.

slides.title: Build a feature: the repayment burden
says: Loan plus 15 percent charges, shared over the months, divided by income.
A burden of 0.29 means the instalment takes 29 percent of income.
slides.notes:
We can also build a new feature from the old ones. Data scientists call this feature engineering. In a spreadsheet you'd call it adding a calculated column.

Our question is simple. How heavy is the monthly instalment compared with what the borrower earns? Take the loan amount, add fifteen percent for interest and charges, divide by the number of months, then divide by monthly income.

The typical loan has a burden of point two nine. That means the instalment eats twenty nine percent of income. The heaviest burden in the file is over nine. That borrower faces an instalment of more than nine times their monthly income.

Does this number tell us anything about default? Let's draw it.

slides.title: Default climbs steeply with repayment burden
look: The lightest fifth of burdens default 4.8 percent of the time.
Default rises slowly through the middle.
The heaviest fifth defaults 31.7 percent of the time.
slides.caption: Borrowers split into fifths by burden. The top fifth defaults about 6.6 times as often as the bottom fifth.
slides.alt: Bar chart showing default rate rising with repayment burden.
slides.notes:
We split the borrowers into five equal groups by burden, lightest to heaviest, and worked out the default rate in each.

In the lightest group, four point eight percent default. Not many.

Through the middle groups the rate creeps up, from five point seven to about eleven percent.

Then the heaviest fifth jumps to thirty one point seven percent. Nearly one borrower in three. That's about six and a half times the rate of the lightest group.

So the burden column carries signal. A model can only learn from what we show it, and a well chosen column often does more than a fancier method.

slides.title: Choose features, leave one column out
slides.code:
features = ['age', 'monthly_income_ugx', 'income_missing',
            'loan_amount_ugx', 'term_months', 'previous_loans',
            'previous_late_payments', 'group_loan',
            'savings_balance_ugx', 'has_mobile_money',
            'distance_to_branch_km', 'burden']
# collection_calls is left out on purpose.
X = loans[features]
y = loans['default']
print(X.shape, y.shape)
says: Twelve input columns go into X, a table of features.
y holds the target, the column default.
slides.notes:
Time to separate the features from the target. By convention a capital X holds the features, and a small y holds the target.

We list twelve columns by name. The list includes our new burden, our income flag and the cleaned age and income. The target goes in y.

The comment in the code matters. The file has a column called collection_calls, and I'm leaving it out on purpose. Session 16 explains why, and the reason surprises most people. For today, leave it out too.

Check the shapes. X has eight thousand rows and twelve columns, and y has eight thousand values. Same rows, same order. That's the pairing the computer needs.

slides.title: Hold back a test set before the model sees anything
look: Most loans go in the training set.
A smaller part is locked away as the test set.
We open the test set once, at the end.
slides.caption: Here: 6,000 loans to learn from and 2,000 kept hidden.
slides.alt: A long bar divided into a larger training part and a smaller test part held back.
slides.notes:
Splitting the data is the most important habit in this module, so here is why we do it.

Imagine a student who gets the exam paper a week early and memorises the answers. Full marks on the exam tells you nothing about what they understand. A model is the same. If we score it on the loans it learned from, we only learn that it can remember.

So before the model sees anything, we cover part of the data with a sheet of paper. In Excel terms, hide the last rows and promise not to peek.

The big part is the training set. The model learns here. The smaller part is the test set, locked away until the end. We use it once, and the score on it is our best guess of how the model will do on tomorrow's loans.

Here, six thousand loans to learn from and two thousand to test on.

slides.title: Split the data with train_test_split
slides.code:
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.25, stratify=y, random_state=42)
says: test_size=0.25 hides a quarter of the loans: 2,000 of 8,000.
stratify=y keeps about 12.5 percent defaults in both parts.
random_state=42 makes the shuffle repeatable.
slides.notes:
From here on the code needs scikit-learn, which is free and already installed in Colab. You'll run it in the lab.

The function is train_test_split. We give it X and y, and it hands back four things: the training features, the test features, the training targets and the test targets. Always in that order.

test_size of point two five hides a quarter of the loans, so two thousand are kept for testing.

stratify equals y makes sure the training and test parts both keep about twelve and a half percent defaults. Without it, a lucky or unlucky shuffle could leave the test set with too few defaults to judge anything.

random_state is a seed. It fixes the shuffle, so you and I get the same split. Any number works. Forty two is a tradition.

slides.title: The baseline: always say no default
slides.code:
from sklearn.dummy import DummyClassifier

baseline = DummyClassifier(strategy='most_frequent')
baseline.fit(X_train, y_train)
print(baseline.score(X_test, y_test))
says: The dummy learns only the most common answer: 0.
fit means learn from the training data.
score gives the share of test loans it got right.
slides.notes:
Before we build a clever model, we build a stupid one. A baseline is the score of a guesser that learns nothing.

DummyClassifier with the setting most frequent always gives the most common answer in the training data. Here that's zero, no default, for every single loan. In a spreadsheet it's like forecasting next month by repeating this month.

Fit is the word for learning. The dummy fits the training data, which for it just means counting.

Score gives the accuracy on the test set. Accuracy is the share of loans where the answer was right. Because about eighty seven and a half percent of loans are repaid, this lazy guesser scores close to that. Expect a number between eighty six and eighty eight percent. Your run may differ from mine by a little.

This number is the bar. Every model we build has to beat it.

slides.title: Fit a first model and predict
slides.code:
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier

first = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=3, random_state=42)
first.fit(X_train, y_train)
pred = first.predict(X_test)
print(first.score(X_test, y_test))
says: Choose a model and keep its settings small.
fit learns from the training set. predict answers for the test loans.
score compares the answers with the truth.
slides.notes:
Now a model that learns something. The code changes very little: choose a model, fit it, predict with it. That pattern runs through almost every model in scikit-learn.

The model here is a small decision tree. Don't worry about how it works. We open it in Session 15. Today only the pattern matters.

Fit hands the model the training features and the true answers. It learns.

Predict hands it the test features only, with no answers, and it returns a guess of zero or one for each of the two thousand test loans.

Score compares those guesses with the truth we kept hidden. You should land close to the baseline, somewhere between eighty five and ninety percent. Probably only a little above the lazy guesser, and that's a finding in itself. The trap for today explains why.

slides.title: A high score that proves nothing
slides.looks: Your first model scores about eighty seven percent on the test set. That sounds excellent, and nothing warns you.
slides.why: Always answering no default also scores about eighty seven percent, because only one loan in eight defaults. The model may have learned very little.
slides.fix: Print the baseline score beside the model score every time. Session 16 gives scores that suit rare events.
slides.notes:
Today's trap runs without any error.

You fit your first model, and it scores about eighty seven percent on the test set. You feel clever. Eighty seven percent would be a fine mark in most exams.

But look at what the lazy guesser scored on the same loans. About the same. The model has just matched a guesser who never looks at any borrower.

The reason is class imbalance. When only one loan in eight defaults, answering no every time is right most of the time, and it catches no defaults at all. The score hides that.

To fix it, print the baseline next to the model score every time. If your model cannot beat the baseline, it hasn't earned a place yet. In Session 16 we meet scores that look at the rare defaults directly.

slides.title: A misspelt column name stops the build
slides.code:
raw = pd.read_csv('loans.csv')
raw['burden'] = raw.loan_amount_ugx * 1.15 / raw.term_months / raw.monthly_income
says: Read the last line first. The column is monthly_income_ugx.
slides.notes:
Preparing data is where most of your errors will happen, so let's read one together.

We rebuild the burden, but we type monthly income and forget the underscore ugx at the end.

Python stops, and the last line says the data frame has no attribute called monthly income. Remember Session 5. Read the last line first. It says the column doesn't exist under that name.

The cure is to print loans dot columns and copy the name exactly. Column names in a CSV are fussy. One missing letter and the whole line fails.

slides.title: Today's steps on the workflow loop
look: Question, data and features come first.
Split, train and evaluate follow, in that order.
A weak result sends us round the loop again.
slides.caption: Most of the work sits in the first three boxes.
slides.alt: A loop of steps: question, data, features, split, train, evaluate, then improve or deliver.
slides.notes:
Let's put the whole session on one picture. This loop is the machine learning workflow, and you'll walk round it again in every session until the end of the module.

It starts with a question. Will this borrower default? Then the data, the eight thousand loans. Then the features, where we cleaned the ages, filled the incomes and built the burden.

Then the split, with a test set locked away. Then training, where the model learns. Then evaluate, the gold box, where we score on the test set and compare with the baseline.

The red arrow is the way back. If the result is weak, we go back round. Better features, a different model, a closer look at the question. Real projects loop many times.

Notice how much of today went into the first three boxes. That's normal. Most of the work is the data.
